title: Finding the Minimum Eating Speed to Finish Bananas

phrases.explanation: Before a deadline or time limit expires
Equal to or greater than a certain speed
Reduce the range of possible answers step by step
Try every possible value one by one without optimization
The most important observation that leads to a better solution

technical_terms.definition: An algorithm that repeatedly halves a sorted search space to find a target value efficiently
The range of all possible candidate answers we need to examine
A function that always increases or always decreases, never changing direction
Division that rounds up to the nearest whole number instead of rounding down

concept: Given an array of banana piles and a number h representing available hours, find the minimum integer eating speed k such that all bananas can be eaten within h hours. At speed k, each hour you eat k bananas from one pile. If a pile has fewer than k bananas, you finish that pile and wait for the next hour.

solutions.label: Linear Search
solutions.summary: Try every speed from 1 up to the maximum pile size. For each speed, check if all piles can be finished within h hours.

solutions.label: Binary Search on Speed
solutions.summary: Use binary search over the range of possible speeds from 1 to max pile size. For each candidate speed, compute total hours needed and adjust the search range accordingly.

sections.title: Understanding the Problem
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    style A fill:#f87171,color:#fff
    style B fill:#f87171,color:#fff
    A["Piles: [3, 6, 7, 11]"]
    B["Hours available: h = 8"]
    A --> C["Find minimum speed k"]
    B --> C
    C --> D["k = 4: pile 3→1hr, pile 6→2hr, pile 7→2hr, pile 11→3hr"]
    D --> E["Total = 8 hours ✓"]

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Here's the scenario. Imagine you have several piles of bananas, represented as an integer array. You also have h hours before a deadline. You need to find the minimum eating speed, let's call it k, so that you can finish all the bananas within h hours. Each hour, you pick one pile and eat up to k bananas from it. If a pile has fewer than k bananas left, you finish it and wait until the next hour.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Got it. So each hour I can only eat from one pile, and even if I finish early, I can't start the next pile until the next hour. Can I confirm the constraints? The array will always have at least one pile, and h is always greater than or equal to the number of piles?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Exactly. h is guaranteed to be at least the length of the piles array, so a valid answer always exists. Pile values are positive integers.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Let me confirm with an example. If piles are three, six, seven, eleven and h is eight, at speed four: pile three takes one hour, pile six takes two hours, pile seven takes two hours, pile eleven takes three hours. That totals eight hours, which fits. And speed three would need more than eight hours, so the answer is four.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: That's correct. The answer for that example is four. Go ahead and think about how you'd solve this.

sections.title: Linear Search Through All Speeds
sections.diagram:
graph LR
    style S1 fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style S2 fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style S3 fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style S4 fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    S1["k=1: 27hrs ✗"] --> S2["k=2: 16hrs ✗"]
    S2 --> S3["k=3: 9hrs ✗"]
    S3 --> S4["k=4: 8hrs ✓ → answer!"]

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The simplest approach is a linear search. The minimum possible speed is one, and the maximum useful speed is the largest pile, which is eleven in our example. I try each speed starting from one and check if the total hours needed is within h.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: For each speed k, I go through every pile and calculate the hours needed using ceiling division. That's pile plus k minus one, divided by k. I sum up all the hours. If the total is less than or equal to h, that k is my answer since I'm checking from the smallest value upward.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: What's the time complexity of this approach?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: It's O of max piles times n, where n is the number of piles. For each candidate speed up to the max pile value, I iterate through all n piles. Space complexity is O of one since I only use a few variables. This works but is slow when pile values are very large.

sections.title: Binary Search on the Answer
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    style A fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style B fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style C fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style D fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style E fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    A["Search range: lo=1, hi=11"] --> B["mid=6: hours=6 ≤ 8 → hi=6"]
    B --> C["lo=1, hi=6, mid=3: hours=9 > 8 → lo=4"]
    C --> D["lo=4, hi=6, mid=5: hours=7 ≤ 8 → hi=5"]
    D --> E["lo=4, hi=5, mid=4: hours=8 ≤ 8 → hi=4"]
    E --> F["lo=4, hi=4 → answer is 4"]

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The key insight here is that the relationship between speed and total hours is monotonic. As speed increases, total hours decreases. This means I can binary search on the answer instead of checking every value.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: I set lo to one and hi to the max pile value, eleven. I calculate mid as lo plus hi minus lo divided by two. For mid equals six, total hours is six, which is within eight, so I set hi to six. For mid equals three, total hours is nine, which exceeds eight, so I set lo to four.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Continuing, mid equals five gives seven hours, so hi becomes five. Then mid equals four gives exactly eight hours, so hi becomes four. Now lo equals hi equals four, and that's our answer.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Time complexity is O of n times log of max piles. The binary search runs log of max piles iterations, and each feasibility check scans all n piles. Space is still O of one. This is a big improvement when pile values are large.

sections.title: Summary
sections.diagram:
graph LR
    subgraph Comparison
    A["Linear Search\nO of max piles times n\nSimple but slow"] --> B["Binary Search\nO of n log max piles\nOptimal solution"]
    end
    style A fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style B fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Great job. You identified that this is a binary search on the answer problem. The monotonic relationship between speed and hours is the crucial observation that lets us move from linear search to binary search.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Exactly. The pattern of binary searching over possible answers applies whenever we have a yes-no feasibility check that flips at a single threshold. The ceiling division trick for computing hours per pile is also a useful technique to remember.
